name: What AI Does Well
title: What AI Does Well
answer: AI is strongest at repetitive, language-heavy work that a person can easily check, which covers a surprising share of a school day. The best results come when AI supports a skilled adult rather than replacing one, with the adult designing how the tool is used and staying present while it runs. Gains from such programs can be real but may not last, so the human role in teaching remains central.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: This idea sets out what AI does well so that schools can aim it at the right tasks and keep people in charge of the rest. AI performs best on work that repeats, involves a lot of language, and is simple for a person to verify, and in schools that covers more of the day than many expect, from parent letters to lunch counts. The book presents six strengths that recur most often in this Volume, each paired with the part of the work a person still performs. The point of the pairing is that no AI output counts as finished until someone checks it. The idea solves the problem of schools either dismissing AI entirely or handing it work it cannot safely complete alone.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a Southern US district, 900 new tutors working with 1,800 students were given an AI assistant that suggested what to say next, and the AI spoke to the tutor rather than the student. In Nigeria, students around age 15 worked in pairs with an AI chat tool in after school sessions across six weeks, with teachers opening each session using a prompt that told the AI to act as a tutor rather than an answer machine and walking the room throughout. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond these settings. In both cases adults designed how the AI would be used and remained in the room while it operated. Neither program turned students loose with a chatbot.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports two studies. In the Southern US district, students whose tutors had the AI assistant were 4 percentage points more likely to master a topic, and students of tutors who actually used it gained 14 points, at a cost of about $20 per tutor per year, though end of year state test scores did not rise (Wang et al., 2024). In Nigeria, students gained 0.31 standard deviations, described as one of the larger effects measured for a program that short (De Simone et al., 2025). The book treats these as the best results so far and notes that short gains do not always last. It also stresses that the tutors, not the software, did the teaching.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. AI is only suited to work that is repetitive, language-heavy, and easy for a person to check, and every strength listed comes with a part of the work a person still does, because nothing is finished until someone checks it. Gains may be short lived, as the district results show when state test scores did not move. Success did not come from leaving students alone with a chatbot, and the adults, not the software, did the teaching. The decisions about how the AI is used, what it is asked to do, and what happens with its output stay with the people in the room.
